name: Guavas
tile_uses: Raw with salt and chile, with queso fresco, the drink
why_now: Guavas ripen in San Diego backyards from late summer into winter, and October is when they fill the bins at Mexican markets and farm stands. Pink-fleshed and fragrant, they're the most tropical thing in a fall basket — a reminder that fall here isn't New England.
how_to_choose: Smell first: a ripe guava is fragrant from a foot away
Pale yellow-green skin, turning from hard green
A slight give when pressed, like a ripe pear
Small brown marks are fine; soft, wet spots are not
buy_this_much: 5–6. Some ripe now, some firmer for later in the week.
price_note: Much cheaper at Mexican markets, where they're sold as guayaba.

flavor_paths.name: With chile and lime
flavor_paths.description: Sliced, a squeeze of lime, salt, chile. The corner-stand way.

flavor_paths.name: With cheese
flavor_paths.description: Queso fresco or a sharp white cheese. Sweet against salty, the classic pairing.

flavor_paths.name: On breakfast
flavor_paths.description: Sliced over yogurt with a little honey.

weekday_uses: Sliced with lime, salt, and Tajín in the afternoon
With queso fresco and a tortilla
weekend_use: Sliced on a plate with queso fresco and new dates, after the fish.
storage: On the counter until they're fragrant and give slightly, then in the fridge for three or four days. Their smell travels — keep them in a closed bag.
one_thing_to_learn: You eat all of a guava: the skin, the flesh, and the small hard seeds. Slice it into rounds and don't bother digging anything out. If the seeds bother you, halve it and scoop the smooth outer flesh, leaving the seedy center for the drink.
